item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q006_ubiquitin_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 places Ubiquitin-related proteins (family d.15.1.1; SUNID 54237), UBX domains (d.15.1.2; 54250), and Ras-binding domains (d.15.1.5; 54263) in the Ubiquitin-like superfamily (d.15.1; 54236), within the beta-Grasp fold (d.15; 54235) and alpha-and-beta (a+b) class (d; 53931). Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry across distinct families, with a conserved structural scaffold that has diversified functionally. This is stronger than merely sharing a fold; fold or class membership alone does not establish homology.\n\nBiologically, ubiquitin and some relatives act as covalent modifiers, many UBX domains recruit p97/VCP, and Ras-binding domains mediate recognition of Ras-family GTPases. These roles are not interchangeable. It would be unsafe to annotate UBX or Ras-binding domains as ubiquitin-like conjugatable modifiers, infer ubiquitination or proteasomal targeting from superfamily membership, or transfer p97-binding or Ras-binding specificity across these families. Even the Ubiquitin-related family does not imply that every member is conjugated. The shared scaffold can guide structural comparison and template selection, but specific function requires supporting sequence and interface conservation, domain context, and biochemical evidence for the relevant binding or conjugation activity.","evidence_used":["Pretrained biological knowledge","mcp__scope__search_scop","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=UBX&mode=auto&limit=10","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=Ras-binding&mode=auto&limit=10","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.15.1.1/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.15.1.2/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.15.1.5/parents"]}]}
